rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening 'Till' continues the rejection recounted in 23:83: disbelievers persist in it until death comes.
rows.anchor: Till is understood to follow the end of v. 83, which recounts the dismissive words of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses likewise portray the dead seeking return so they may give charity or do righteous deeds.
rows.anchor: The desire of those who have died to return to the world is also mentioned vividly in 32:12

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators place the plea before death: after addressing God, the dying person asks the soul-taking angels to return him.
rows.anchor: Some commentators understand the plea for return in this verse

rows.speaker: Others (R)
rows.claim: Other commentators place the request after death, when the person has seen the Fire.
rows.anchor: Others understand this request to be spoken after death, after beholding the Fire (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barzakh is an intervening barrier or isthmus, and the dead cannot return to worldly life.
rows.anchor: Behind them is a barrier refers to the truth that they will not return to the life of this world (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh can mean either a barrier or an isthmus between two things.
rows.anchor: Barrier renders barzakh, a word that connotes either a barrier or an isthmus between two things

rows.speaker: Some commentators (Ṭ)
rows.claim: Some commentators explain that the dying person's words are words he could not help uttering.
rows.anchor: Some commentators understand These are words that he speaks to mean, “These are words that he could not but speak” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet announces the world's end and the approaching Judgment.
rows.anchor: The trumpet that signals the end of the world and the impending Judgment is also mentioned in 18:99

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severing of worldly bonds is illustrated elsewhere by a nursing woman forgetting her child and a man fleeing his brother.
rows.anchor: The breaking of worldly bonds is also mentioned in such verses as 22:2: On the day you see it

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reconciles verses that deny and affirm questioning by treating Judgment as a long sequence of states: terror prevents concern for others at some times, while other states allow it.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī raises the point that some verses say people will not question one another, while other verses say they will (e.g., 7:44–50; 37:27–32, 50; 52:25)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary directs readers to its discussion of the scales of deeds at 101:6–9.
rows.anchor: For a discussion of the scales of deeds, see 101:6–9c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'lose their souls' may also be translated as 'lose themselves.'
rows.anchor: Lose their souls could also be rendered “lose themselves.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter makes people view their whole worldly life as no more than a day or hour.
rows.anchor: the experience of the Hereafter causing people to think of their entire life of this world as nothing more than a day or an hour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is generally regarded as Madinan.
rows.anchor: universally considered to be a Madinan

rows.speaker: Some (Āl)
rows.claim: Some say that verse 58 is Makkan.
rows.anchor: although some say v. 58 is Makkan (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title comes from the Light Verse; the surah's mirage, sea-darkness, and lightning parables use light to depict human inner reality.
rows.anchor: Its title comes from the parable in the famous Light Verse (v. 35)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah matters for Islamic metaphysics and art as well as social and legal questions.
rows.anchor: Al-Nūr also is extremely significant not only for Islamic metaphysics and art but also for certain social and legal questions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verses prescribe adultery's punishment and detailed evidentiary standards for conviction.
rows.anchor: Its opening verses deal with the punishment for adultery and lay out in detail the evidentiary standards for finding a person guilty of this crime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–26 address the accusation of adultery against ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet's youngest wife, and the community's response to a slander declared baseless.
rows.anchor: against ʿĀʾishah, the youngest wife of the Prophet, and the response of the Muslim community to what was eventually declared to be a baseless slander

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah sets etiquette for visiting homes, interaction between unrelated men and women, dress and modesty, and privacy at home.
rows.anchor: various rules of etiquette, such as those governing the visiting one another’s homes (vv. 27–29, 61) and the proper comportment between men and women

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some read the phrase about mountains of clouds as describing how the clouds appear.
rows.anchor: Some read from the mountains [of clouds] therein as a reference to the appearance of the clouds

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others parse the phrase grammatically as saying that a mountain's worth of hail descends.
rows.anchor: others read the grammar of the phrase to mean that a “mountain’s worth of hail” comes down

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Hail is interpreted as an instrument of destruction, as with the destructive clouds in 46:24.
rows.anchor: The hail is interpreted here as an instrument of destruction (Th)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Clouds usually bring beneficial rain, which symbolizes spiritual blessings reaching the believer's heart.
rows.anchor: clouds are beneficial givers of rain (7:57; 35:9), and this symbolizes spiritual blessings raining down upon the heart of the believer (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of lightning nearly blinding people also appears in 2:20.
rows.anchor: The image of lightning snatching away sight is also mentioned in 2:20

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators regard al-Furqān as a Makkan surah.
rows.anchor: commentators consider al-Furqān to be a Makkan

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some regard verses 68–70 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: although some believe that vv. 68–70 are from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: A minority
rows.claim: A minority classifies most of the surah as Madinan but verses 68–70 as Makkan.
rows.anchor: while a minority consider most of the sūrah to be from the Madinan period and vv. 68–70 to be from the Makkan period

rows.anchor: be rendered “the Divide,” and which is also

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Furqān is also a name for the Quran.
rows.anchor: a name of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A main theme is Quraysh's refusal to accept Muhammad as prophet because he is human: they object that he walks in markets, lacks treasure, and has no angelic companion.
rows.anchor: he walks in the market like any other human being, is given no great treasure, and is not accompanied by an angel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh also ask why the Quran came gradually instead of all at once.
rows.anchor: why the Quran was not sent down all at once, rather than being revealed gradually over years (v. 32)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their denial also appears in their aversion to God's name al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: part of their denial is manifest in their aversion to the use of the Divine Name al-Raḥmān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers are horrified by the Fire and call to be destroyed rather than endure its punishment.
rows.anchor: the horror of the disbelievers as they call out to be destroyed rather than suffer the punishment of the Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objects worshiped by the disbelievers rebuke and disown them in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: they are rebuked and denied by the objects of their worship in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejected prophets Moses, Aaron, Noah, and the messengers sent to al-Rass serve as historical examples.
rows.anchor: Moses and Aaron, Noah, and the messengers sent to al-Rass are mentioned as previous examples of prophets who were rejected by their people (vv. 35–40)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section teaches believers to face vain talk and insults well, and treats repentance and supplication to God.
rows.anchor: The latter part of the sūrah includes several verses that describe how the believers should conduct themselves in the face of vain talk and insults

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later verses also address the true meaning of repentance and supplication to God.
rows.anchor: addresses the true meaning of repentance and supplication to God (vv. 63–77)
